content: Findings from earlier studies should be interpreted with caution. To provide a clearer understanding, the included studies are presented in chronological order based on the ART (antiretroviral therapy) era. Women living with HIV (WLHIV) have a higher prevalence of HPV and cervical cancer compared to HIV-negative women. The risk of cervical cancer in WLHIV is inversely associated with CD4 count. ART has been shown to reduce the risk of progression to precancerous lesions, particularly after immune system reconstitution (Liu et al., AIDS 2018). Based on three studies of moderate risk of bias, histologically confirmed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) 2/3 was observed in approximately 7% of screened WLHIV under the age of 25 and 11% of those under the age of 30. However, histologically confirmed invasive cervical cancer (ICC) was rare before the age of 35–40. Balancing early detection of cervical precancer in WLHIV with appropriate screening frequency is critical, but there is limited evidence to determine the optimal age or screening test stratification. Data on CIN 2/3, adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), and ICC occurrence are particularly scarce. A systematic review by Rohner et al. (2019) provided additional data on ICC in WLHIV, showing that 8–29% of incident ICC cases in WLHIV were diagnosed before the age of 30. However, the lack of population denominator counts prevented the calculation of prevalence or pooling with other studies. Regarding rescreening intervals for WLHIV who had a negative first screening test for cervical precancer, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether rescreening should occur within 1, 2, or 3 years. Heterogeneity in reporting standards and follow-up durations across studies further complicates data synthesis. For WLHIV treated for cervical precancer lesions and subsequently screened negative at 1-year follow-up, the risk of recurrence is higher compared to HIV-negative women. A systematic review (de Beaudrap et al., Clinical Infectious Diseases 2019) confirmed increased recurrence rates of lesions in WLHIV after treatment. However, no studies specifically addressed the risk of recurrence or the appropriate frequency of rescreening following a first negative test after treatment. Indirect evidence from studies involving cryotherapy or LLETZ (large loop excision of the transformation zone) showed consistently higher recurrence rates in WLHIV compared to HIV-negative women. There is a significant gap in the literature regarding age-specific data in narrow age bands to analyze lesion frequency and follow-up after positive or negative screening tests. Additionally, no studies were identified that reported on the risk of recurrence following a first negative test after treatment, nor on the harms, costs, or cost-effectiveness of screening as a function of age and frequency in WLHIV. Similarly, no studies explored women’s preferences and values regarding these options. There is a clear need for further research in this area. An individual patient data meta-analysis is planned to provide age-specific evidence on cervical cancer screening initiation and frequency, including treatment follow-up.
